title: Statista gave up most of its 35 million monthly search users to keep its data away from AI
excerpt: Statista’s Marc Berg told in our TNW Podcast why it put its data behind a registration wall, and how customers now use it in AI tools.
content_html:
Statista used to get about 35 million monthly active users from search, for free. Then AI crawlers started taking its data straight into chatbot answers, and the company put almost everything behind a registration wall, CEO Marc Berg told me. Its search traffic fell to about 8 million.

“It was a very hard decision for us to say this is not the value of the company, the value of the company is the data.” Marc Berg, Statista

Berg has been leading Statista, the global data company founded and headquartered in Hamburg, for three years. We recorded this episode of TNW Podcast at Web Summit in Lisbon. He also gave a talk there on the same decision. Earlier episodes featured Ronan Harris of Snap, Jennifer Burns of Bright Data, and Danila Shtan of Nebius. The full conversation is in the video below.

From aggregator to data producer

Statista helps companies understand consumer markets: who buys what, how big a market is and who the competitors are, Berg said. Its clients include consulting and marketing agencies and consumer goods companies.

The company started by aggregating existing data, and it has partnerships with about 11,000 data providers. Over the past six years it has invested heavily in its own data. It built a global consumer panel with more than three million interviews and market models for more than 1,000 industries. Today about 70% of its data is proprietary, he said.

Two former consultants founded Statista in Hamburg almost 20 years ago, with no venture or private equity money. They grew it to 160 million in revenue within 12 years and almost 1,400 employees, Berg said. They sold it seven years ago to a publicly listed German media group, which still owns it and is also a customer.

The crawlers came for the data

To grow without outside money, Statista leaned on search, Berg said. It let Google crawl its proprietary content, and showed the first page view for free. Visitors had to sign in to come back, which generated leads.

That opened the door to AI crawlers too. Statista’s data ended up in chatbot answers, cited as a source. Customers started asking why they should pay Statista when a ChatGPT subscription costs about $19 a month.

Statista blocked the crawlers, but robots.txt files did not stop all players, he said. So the company moved its data behind a registration wall.

“So we are willing to sacrifice all the traffic, or a large part of the traffic, in order to protect our data, and we have to find a different way to monetize it.” Marc Berg, Statista

AI companies then came to Statista, he said, asking why one of their most cited sources had disappeared. That led to cooperation talks.

Bring your own license

Statista now sells access through Statista Connect, an API and MCP server that plugs its data into Claude, Copilot or ChatGPT. Customers keep a contract with Statista and bring that license to whichever AI tool they use. They buy credits up front, and proprietary data costs more per credit than third-party data that Statista only structures.

Usage is growing 25 to 30 times year over year, Berg said. While only 2% of existing customers moved to the new offering so far, 70% of customers with a Connect license are already using it.

A consultant building a chart on sneaker sales in Italy can pull analyst-verified Statista data straight into PowerPoint through Copilot. Beyond individual charts, Copilot can also use that data to generate a full market-entry deck, including market sizing.

The change cost Statista revenue. Its lead pipeline dried up, although it only converted about 0.01% of its search traffic. Some smaller customers, with up to 50 employees, left because a chatbot answer was good enough for them. The enterprise business is growing, he said.

Correct answers are the next battleground

Berg no longer writes five-year strategies. Statista plans 12 months ahead, based on assumptions it keeps challenging. Most AI models are now comparable for research, he said, so the competition will be over whether their answers are correct. That matters more as agents run without people checking their work.

“You have to have proprietary, high-quality and exclusive data that is fresh and can be traceable. And then you have a moat.” Marc Berg, Statista

Statista is investing in metadata, context, skills and evals around its data. Through a partner, it also has access to trillions of credit card transactions, which it uses to model e-commerce markets.

Building European companies

Berg says he is not a founder and likes building and scaling teams, especially in Europe. He has a track record of helping European tech companies scale, from Klarna to FreeNow and now Statista.

He thinks Europe’s environment is built for stability, not innovation. Stock options are taxed like normal income, labour laws make it hard to scale a company up and down, and regulation such as GDPR adds compliance work, he said.
